title: Block close: the wilderness road
hook: slaves, sea, manna, mountain, calf, and forty years of being carried

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah, and Jesus hanging all the law on two commandments. Your line was on these two hang all. Did you ask the two-hinge question? Day four hundred eleven, and the close of the wilderness road.

Five weeks ago, this path opened on a people making bricks for a king who had forgotten them. Since then: two midwives who said no. A basket in the reeds. A bush on fire that didn't burn up, and a name, I AM. Ten plagues and a night of blood on the doorposts. A sea that opened. A tambourine. Bread on the ground every morning. Thunder on a mountain, ten words, a golden calf, and the back of God passing by. Corners of fields, a jubilee horn, twelve spies, a talking donkey, and an old man on Mount Nebo looking at a land he would never enter. Today we stand at the end of that road and look back.
screen: `BRICKS FOR A KING WHO FORGOT.` → `A SEA, A MOUNTAIN, A CALF.` → `TODAY WE LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew name for the book of Numbers is Bemidbar: in the wilderness. And for these four books, that's where the people mostly are. Not in Egypt anymore. Not in the land yet. In between. It's a long, hard in-between. They complain, constantly. About the water, the food, Moses, the giants. They make a calf the moment Moses is late. A whole generation is too afraid to go in. If you read these books looking for heroes, you'll be disappointed by almost everyone, including, at Meribah, Moses himself. But read them again and notice who keeps showing up. Manna every morning, even on the mornings after they grumbled. Water from a rock. A pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Clothes that didn't wear out. Here's how Moses sums it up in Deuteronomy, in the King James Bible: "in the wilderness, where thou hast seen how that the LORD thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went, until ye came into this place." Bare thee: carried you. Like a father carrying a tired child on his shoulders the last mile home. That's the thread through the whole road. Not that the people were strong, or faithful, or patient. They mostly weren't. It's that they were carried. Christians have read their own lives in this road for two thousand years: rescued from slavery, but not home yet; fed one day at a time; failing, and carried anyway. Many traditions call the time between baptism and heaven a pilgrimage, and Lent's forty days echo the forty years. And tomorrow we open the songbook those carried people and their children would one day sing: the Psalms.
screen: `BEMIDBAR: IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `ALMOST NO HEROES.` · `MANNA, EVEN AFTER GRUMBLING.` · `CARRIED, AS A MAN BEARS HIS SON.` · then, large: `THE LORD THY GOD BARE THEE, AS A MAN DOTH BEAR HIS SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your own wilderness season. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a stretch of your life that was in-between: out of one thing and not yet into the next. A move. A job lost. An illness. A breakup. A long wait. Name it, simply. Then look for the manna. What kept showing up, day by day, even when you were grumbling? A friend. A routine. A small mercy. Someone's casserole. Notice that you came through. If you pray, you can thank God for carrying you. If not, thank whoever did. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of the wilderness road: from slavery, through the sea and the long desert years, to the edge of the land, carried the whole way.
Your line: carried through the desert. Today, tell one person about a hard season you came through, and who carried you. Day four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Many Christians describe hard seasons as 'wilderness' times, and churches often link the forty days of Lent to Israel's forty years in the desert and Jesus' forty days of fasting.

what it means: the in-between, out of slavery and not yet home, where a grumbling people were fed daily and carried.
what a scholar hears: Bemidbar, the book's Hebrew name; Deuteronomy 1:31's father carrying his son; and Lent's forty days echoing the forty years.
